content: Relevant authorities, such as the police or protection officers, should be involved in cases of violence against women only when necessary. Exceptions to this include situations where mandatory reporting is required by law, such as cases involving minors subjected to abuse or when the life of a woman experiencing violence is in immediate danger. The WHO (2013) emphasizes these exceptions, and the Essential Services Package further recommends prohibiting mandatory reporting of individual cases between coordinating agencies unless there is immediate danger, child victims, or special vulnerabilities (UN Women et al., 2015). The collection and management of administrative data on violence against women (VAW) must adhere to national and sectoral privacy regulations, as well as international standards. These standards require informing individuals about how their personally identifiable information will be used, with whom it will be shared, and under what circumstances. If personal data is to be used for secondary purposes, such as statistical analysis, this must align with legal frameworks, protect individual privacy, and serve the best interests of the individuals or groups involved. During the collection of VAW administrative data, individuals must be explicitly informed and provide consent for their information to be shared for care and management purposes. They should also be informed that aggregate, non-identifiable data will be used to improve VAW policies and programs. If individuals do not consent to their information being recorded, their wishes must be respected without denying them care or services. Policies and procedures must be implemented to protect the confidentiality and personal data of survivors and alleged perpetrators at every stage, from data collection to storage, processing, analysis, and communication. All staff involved in documenting and managing VAW administrative data must be trained in these policies and procedures, commit to their implementation, and understand the consequences of non-compliance. Data collection systems should be designed with a survivor-centered approach, ensuring that documentation does not create barriers to receiving services. Survivors must have the autonomy to decline having their information recorded without fear of losing access to services. Data collection forms and information management systems should allow for non-response by survivors, including options such as declined to answer to distinguish from missing data. The number of questions asked should be minimized, and only the essential data should be collected. Questions should avoid implying blame or stigmatizing survivors and should be asked with empathy, only when necessary, and with clear explanations of their purpose. Survivors should always have the option to decline answering. Documentation should focus only on information relevant to service provision and avoid collecting unnecessary details that could lead to prejudice or discrimination against survivors during service provision or legal processes. For example, information on drug and alcohol use or mental health status should only be documented if it is directly relevant to providing services. Survivors should not be questioned about their sexual history. The legal framework and social context will determine which socio-demographic variables are safe to collect, with the minimum data set including the survivor's sex, age, relationship with the perpetrator, and the location of the violence. Access to individual records of VAW survivors should be limited to those directly involved in care provision or responsible for aggregating and reporting data. Supervisors and decision-makers should only access anonymized, aggregate data. Data management practices must follow best practices for data protection and security, ensuring that any public data is anonymized to prevent identification of individuals. VAW administrative data can be used to monitor service use, assess policy implementation, and improve service coverage and quality. It can also inform resource allocation and system planning. However, it is important to recognize the limitations of VAW administrative data, such as its inability to provide prevalence rates of violence against women. Less than 40% of survivors seek help, and most turn to family and friends rather than institutional support. Less than 10% of survivors report to the police. Service-use data provides insights into the demand for services and can help identify gaps in service delivery. During the COVID-19 pandemic, VAW administrative data played a critical role in shaping and monitoring emergency responses to VAW. Countries used this data to allocate resources, strengthen hotline coverage, and prioritize VAW cases in courts. Some countries introduced targeted social protection and economic support for survivors. The pandemic highlighted the importance of real-time data for guiding policy and programmatic responses. To improve the collection and use of VAW administrative data, leadership and coordination are essential. A national or subnational coordination mechanism can define roles and responsibilities, improve data quality, and catalyze political and operational support. This mechanism should include representatives from relevant sectors, such as the police, justice, health, and civil society organizations (CSOs), and should prioritize survivor-centered approaches and data protection. Morocco provides an example of a national coordination mechanism through its National Commission for the Care of Women Victims of Violence, established under a 2018 law. This commission coordinates efforts across sectors, monitors and evaluates action plans, and reports on outcomes. It has recommended creating unified VAW indicators, developing an intersectoral administrative data system, and ensuring alignment with national data protection laws.
